articles.label: Investigation
articles.headline: Escambia County's $2.3M tourism contract renewed without public bid
articles.dek: The county commission voted 4-1 last month to extend Visit Pensacola's marketing agreement through 2029. Three commissioners received campaign contributions from board members of the tourism agency.
brief: Escambia County commissioners voted 4-1 in June to extend Visit Pensacola's $2.3 million annual marketing contract through 2029 without issuing a competitive bid
Three of the four commissioners who voted yes received campaign contributions totaling $14,500 from Visit Pensacola board members since 2022
Commissioner Marcus DeLeon cast the lone dissenting vote, calling the no-bid process 'a disservice to taxpayers who deserve to know we're getting the best deal'
articles.body:
The vote took eleven minutes. No members of the public spoke. When it was done, Escambia County had committed $11.5 million in tourist development taxes over the next five years to an organization whose board members had written checks to three of the four commissioners who approved the deal.

The June 18 commission meeting moved through routine business before reaching agenda item 14B: a five-year contract extension for Visit Pensacola, the nonprofit destination marketing organization that has held the county's tourism promotion contract since 2015. The item had been placed on the consent agenda, meaning it would have passed without discussion had Commissioner Marcus DeLeon not pulled it for separate consideration.

"I want to understand why we're not putting this out for bid," DeLeon said, according to meeting minutes. "$2.3 million a year is not pocket change."

County Administrator Wes Moreno explained that Florida statute allows for sole-source contracts when an organization provides unique services. Visit Pensacola, he said, had institutional knowledge and established relationships with travel industry partners that would be difficult to replicate.

DeLeon pressed further. Had the county evaluated other destination marketing firms? Had it compared Visit Pensacola's performance metrics to industry benchmarks? Moreno acknowledged that no formal evaluation had been conducted.

The vote proceeded: Commissioners Lumon May, Doug Underhill, Jeff Bergosh and Steven Barry voted yes. DeLeon voted no.

Following the money

Campaign finance records filed with the Escambia County Supervisor of Elections show a pattern of contributions from Visit Pensacola board members to the commissioners who approved the contract.

Commissioner May received $6,000 across four contributions from Visit Pensacola board members between January 2022 and March 2026. The donors include Quint Studer, the healthcare entrepreneur and downtown Pensacola developer who chairs Visit Pensacola's board, and Lewis Bear Jr., whose family operates the region's largest beer distributorship.

Commissioner Bergosh received $5,000 from three board members over the same period. Commissioner Barry received $3,500 from two board members.

Commissioner DeLeon, who cast the dissenting vote, received no contributions from Visit Pensacola board members. Commissioner Underhill received $1,000 from Studer in 2023.

None of these contributions violate Florida campaign finance law, which caps individual donations at $1,000 per election cycle. The Flightline found no evidence that any commissioner explicitly tied their vote to contributions received.

When contacted for comment, Commissioner May said the contributions had no bearing on his vote.

"I've supported Visit Pensacola because they do excellent work for our community," May said in an email. "My campaign contributors include hundreds of people from all sectors. To suggest that a few donations influenced a policy decision is insulting."

Commissioners Bergosh and Barry did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Studer, the Visit Pensacola board chair, declined to comment through a spokesperson.

What the contract covers

Visit Pensacola operates under a contract funded by the county's Tourist Development Tax, a 5% levy on short-term rentals that generated $47.2 million in fiscal year 2025. Under the renewed agreement, Visit Pensacola will receive $2.3 million annually—roughly 4.9% of total TDT revenue—for marketing, advertising and destination promotion.

The organization's stated mission is to increase visitation to Escambia County through national advertising campaigns, trade show attendance, travel writer outreach and digital marketing. According to its most recent annual report, Visit Pensacola's efforts contributed to 6.2 million visitors spending $3.1 billion in the county in 2025.

Those figures come from Tourism Economics, a consulting firm contracted by Visit Pensacola to estimate visitor impact. The methodology relies on surveys, hotel occupancy data and economic modeling. Independent verification of the spending estimates is not possible with publicly available data.

The contract requires Visit Pensacola to submit quarterly reports to the county and maintain an annual audit. The Flightline reviewed the past three years of audits; all were conducted by the same Pensacola-based accounting firm that Visit Pensacola has used since 2016.

Industry standards and questions

Destination marketing contracts vary widely across Florida counties. Some, like Hillsborough and Pinellas, issue competitive bids every five to seven years. Others, like Escambia, rely on long-term relationships with established organizations.

"There's no single right approach," said Dr. Rachel Kinney, a professor of hospitality management at the University of Central Florida who studies destination marketing organizations. "But best practice in the field is periodic competitive review, even if you end up renewing with the same organization. It keeps everyone honest."

Kinney noted that $2.3 million would likely attract interest from regional and national destination marketing firms if put to bid.

"That's a substantial budget," she said. "You'd have several firms competing for that work."

The last time Escambia County issued a competitive bid for destination marketing services was 2008, when the Tourist Development Council recommended creating a new public-private partnership. Visit Pensacola, then called the Pensacola Bay Area Convention and Visitors Bureau, emerged from that process.

Since then, the contract has been renewed four times without a public bid—in 2012, 2016, 2021 and now 2026.

DeLeon's objection

In an interview with The Flightline, Commissioner DeLeon said his vote was about process, not performance.

"I'm not saying Visit Pensacola does a bad job," he said. "I'm saying we have an obligation to verify that through competition. When you hand someone $11 million without checking the market, you're trusting instead of verifying."

DeLeon said he requested a competitive bid process before the June meeting but was told by county staff that there was insufficient time to conduct one before the current contract expired in September.

"That's a planning failure," he said. "We knew for five years this contract was coming up. We had time to do this right."

County Administrator Moreno disputed that characterization. In an email, he said staff began discussing renewal options with Visit Pensacola in early 2026 and determined that continuity of service was the priority.

"A transition to a new vendor would require a minimum of six months for onboarding," Moreno wrote. "The commission determined that uninterrupted destination marketing was in the county's best interest."

What comes next

The renewed contract runs through September 2029. Under its terms, either party can terminate with 180 days notice. Performance benchmarks include maintaining hotel occupancy rates above the state average and achieving specified reach metrics for advertising campaigns.

If Visit Pensacola fails to meet benchmarks in two consecutive years, the county can open negotiations for early termination. To date, that provision has never been invoked.

DeLeon said he plans to propose a policy requiring competitive bids for all contracts exceeding $1 million, regardless of vendor history. He has not yet secured support from other commissioners.

"I may be a minority of one on this," he said. "But the public record will show I asked the question."

The Flightline submitted public records requests for all correspondence between county commissioners and Visit Pensacola board members regarding the contract renewal. As of publication, those requests remain pending.

articles.label: Development & Infrastructure
articles.headline: Six months after the Cervantes Street redesign: faster traffic, more pedestrian close calls
articles.dek: City data shows vehicle speeds up 12% on the corridor. Two crosswalk removals have forced walkers into longer routes or risky crossings. Business owners are split on whether the changes help or hurt.
brief: Average vehicle speeds on Cervantes Street have increased 12% since January's lane reconfiguration, according to city traffic data
The removal of crosswalks at Baylen and Palafox intersections has added 400 feet to pedestrian routes, with some residents crossing mid-block instead
Business owners along the corridor report mixed results—faster drive-by traffic but fewer customers stopping to browse
articles.body:
Maria Santos stood at the corner of Cervantes and Baylen on a Tuesday afternoon, waiting for a gap in traffic that wouldn't come. The crosswalk she'd used for eleven years to reach her bus stop was gone. Painted over in January. Now the nearest legal crossing was two blocks east.

She stepped into the street anyway. A white pickup braked hard. The driver honked.

"I know it's dangerous," Santos said afterward, still catching her breath. "But I'm 67 years old. I can't walk four extra blocks in July."

Six months after Pensacola completed its $2.3 million Cervantes Street redesign, the project has delivered on its primary promise: traffic moves faster. City data obtained by The Flightline shows average vehicle speeds on the corridor have increased from 31 to 35 miles per hour since the January reopening. Rush hour congestion at the I-110 interchange has dropped by roughly eight minutes.

But the redesign has also created new problems the city didn't anticipate—or chose not to prioritize.

The tradeoffs

The project converted a 1.2-mile stretch of Cervantes from four lanes to three, with a center turn lane and widened shoulders the city describes as "future bike infrastructure." Two traffic signals were removed at Baylen and Palafox streets. The crosswalks went with them.

City engineers argued the signals created bottlenecks. Traffic studies from 2024 showed vehicles idling for up to 90 seconds at those intersections during peak hours. Removing them would smooth the flow.

The studies did not measure pedestrian traffic at those crossings.

"We based the design on vehicle level of service," said Robert Hutchins, Pensacola's traffic engineering director, in an interview last week. "Pedestrian counts weren't part of the scope."

Asked why not, Hutchins said the project budget didn't include that analysis. The Florida Department of Transportation, which provided 60% of the funding, set the parameters.

Residents who live north of Cervantes in the Brownsville and Tanyard neighborhoods have felt the impact most acutely. Many rely on bus routes along the corridor. The nearest crosswalks are now at A Street to the west and 9th Avenue to the east—a span of nearly half a mile.

What the data shows

The Flightline reviewed six months of traffic data from city sensors at five points along the corridor. The findings:

Average speeds increased 12% overall, with the largest gains during morning rush hour. The number of vehicles exceeding 40 mph—the posted limit is 35—rose by 23%. At the former Palafox intersection, where a signal once forced stops, average speeds jumped from 28 to 38 mph.

The city does not track pedestrian incidents systematically. But Pensacola Police Department records show officers responded to three pedestrian-involved crashes on Cervantes between January and June 2026. All three occurred at unmarked crossings. One resulted in serious injuries to a 54-year-old man who was struck near Coyle Street in April.

In the same six-month period in 2025, there were zero pedestrian crashes on the corridor.

Three incidents don't constitute a trend. But residents and business owners say near-misses have become routine.

"I see people running across all the time now," said David Park, who owns a laundromat on Cervantes near Baylen. "They're not being reckless. They just don't have anywhere else to go."

Business owners divided

The redesign was sold partly as an economic development tool. Smoother traffic flow, the city argued, would make Cervantes more attractive to drivers and businesses alike.

For some owners, that logic has held.

"My drive-through times are down," said Keisha Brown, manager of the Popeyes on Cervantes near A Street. "Customers get in and out faster. That's good for us."

But businesses that depend on foot traffic or browsing tell a different story.

Janet Odom runs a vintage furniture shop called Second Time Around about 200 feet from the old Baylen crosswalk. She said walk-in customers have dropped by roughly a third since January.

"People used to cross over from the north side, poke around, maybe grab lunch at the sandwich place next door," Odom said. "Now they don't come. The traffic's too fast and there's no safe way over."

Odom attended a city council meeting in March to raise her concerns. She said council members listened politely and moved on.

"I got the sense they'd already made up their minds," she said. "This was about cars. It was always about cars."

What comes next

Pensacola City Council member Delarian Wiggins, whose District 5 includes parts of the Cervantes corridor, said he has received "dozens" of complaints from constituents about the crosswalk removals. He plans to introduce a resolution in August requesting a pedestrian safety study.

"We moved too fast on this," Wiggins said. "We made assumptions about who uses this street and how. Those assumptions were wrong."

Wiggins said he would push for at least one signalized crosswalk to be reinstalled, possibly at Baylen. But he acknowledged the city would need state approval and likely state funding.

Hutchins, the traffic director, said any modifications would require a new traffic study and could take 12 to 18 months to implement.

"We're not opposed to revisiting the design," Hutchins said. "But we have to follow the process."

Maria Santos doesn't have 18 months to wait. She takes the bus to her part-time job at a dry cleaner on Gregory Street three days a week. Every trip starts with that crossing at Baylen.

Last week she bought a reflective vest. Bright yellow. She wears it now when she crosses, hoping drivers will see her in time.

"I shouldn't have to dress like a construction worker to walk to my bus stop," Santos said. "But here we are."

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's housing waitlist hits 14 months as private contractor posts record profits
articles.dek: Navy families are living in extended-stay motels or commuting from Mobile while Balfour Beatty collects $47 million annually to manage base housing. Some units sit vacant, deemed uninhabitable.
brief: Navy families at NAS Pensacola face 14-month waitlists for on-base housing while contractor Balfour Beatty Communities reports record revenues
At least 47 housing units sit vacant and uninhabitable due to mold, structural damage and deferred maintenance
Service members are paying out-of-pocket for extended-stay hotels or commuting up to 90 minutes from Mobile and Crestview
articles.body:
The parking lot at the InTown Suites on Pensacola Boulevard fills up around 1700 every weekday. Half the license plates are out of state. A lot of them have Department of Defense decals.

Aviation Electronics Technician Second Class Marcus Webb has been living in Room 214 for three months. His wife and two kids are back in Virginia Beach, waiting for base housing that was supposed to be ready in April.

"They told us eight to ten weeks when I got orders," Webb said. He was standing outside his door, still in his flight suit. "That was in February. Now they're saying maybe October. Maybe."

Webb pays $1,800 a month for the extended-stay room. His Basic Allowance for Housing covers $2,100. The difference doesn't go far when you're buying groceries at a gas station and doing laundry at a coin-op three blocks away.

He is not alone.

The numbers

According to data obtained through a Freedom of Information Act request, the average wait time for family housing at Naval Air Station Pensacola reached 14.2 months in June 2026. Five years ago, it was 4.7 months.

The waitlist currently holds 847 families. NAS Pensacola has 1,247 housing units under management by Balfour Beatty Communities, the private contractor that has operated military family housing at the base since 2005.

But 47 of those units are offline. Classified as "uninhabitable" in internal maintenance logs, they sit empty while families wait. Mold remediation. Foundation cracks. Electrical systems that haven't been updated since the Reagan administration.

Balfour Beatty's parent company reported $3.2 billion in North American revenue for 2025, with military housing comprising its most profitable segment. The company collects approximately $47 million annually from its NAS Pensacola portfolio alone, according to figures provided by Navy Region Southeast.

A Balfour Beatty spokesperson declined to make anyone available for an interview. In a written statement, the company said it "remains committed to providing quality housing for military families" and that "ongoing capital improvement projects will address deferred maintenance across the portfolio."

The statement did not specify which projects or when they would be completed.

The commute

Some families have stopped waiting.

Chief Aviation Boatswain's Mate Reginald Carson drives 87 miles each way from Mobile. He and his wife bought a house there in December after spending five months on the waitlist with no movement.

"I leave at 0430," Carson said. "Get home around 1900 if nothing goes sideways. My kids are asleep both times."

Carson said three other chiefs in his squadron have made the same choice. One commutes from Crestview. Another from Foley, Alabama.

"The housing office told me I could take a unit in Corry Village," Carson said. Corry Village is the oldest housing area on base, built in 1968. "I went and looked at it. There was black mold behind the toilet. The AC unit was held together with duct tape. I've got a four-year-old with asthma."

He passed.

What the contract says

The Military Housing Privatization Initiative of 1996 was supposed to fix this. The idea was simple: let private developers build and manage housing, and the free market would deliver better results than the Navy ever could.

Thirty years later, the Government Accountability Office has published 14 reports documenting systemic failures in privatized military housing. Mold. Lead paint. Pest infestations. Contractors that collect rent while dodging repairs.

The contract between the Navy and Balfour Beatty for NAS Pensacola runs through 2055. It includes performance metrics, but enforcement has been inconsistent. Between 2021 and 2025, the Navy issued three formal "cure notices" to Balfour Beatty for failing to meet maintenance timelines at the Pensacola installation. None resulted in financial penalties.

Captain Diana Whitfield, commanding officer of Naval Air Station Pensacola, acknowledged the housing situation in a town hall meeting last month.

"We hear you," Whitfield told an audience of about 200 service members and spouses. "We're working with our partners at Balfour Beatty to accelerate the capital improvement timeline."

When a spouse asked what "accelerate" meant in practical terms, Whitfield deferred to a Balfour Beatty representative who was not present.

The gap

The math doesn't work for junior enlisted families.

An E-4 with dependents receives $2,007 per month in BAH for the Pensacola area. The median rent for a three-bedroom apartment in Escambia County hit $1,850 in May, according to Zillow data. That leaves $157 for utilities, renter's insurance and the privilege of competing with University of West Florida students and Pensacola's growing remote-worker population for a shrinking supply of affordable units.

Petty Officer Third Class Alicia Fernandez found an apartment in Brownsville, about 20 minutes from the main gate. She and her husband pay $1,650 for two bedrooms. The complex doesn't take pets. They had to rehome their dog.

"My recruiter told me the Navy takes care of its own," Fernandez said. She laughed, but not like something was funny.

What happens next

Congressman Matt Gaetz's office did not respond to requests for comment. Neither did the offices of Senators Rick Scott or Marco Rubio.

The Navy's inspector general opened an investigation into privatized housing conditions across the Southeast region in March 2026. Results are expected by the end of the fiscal year.

Balfour Beatty has announced plans to renovate 120 units at NAS Pensacola over the next 18 months. At that pace, the 47 uninhabitable units would come back online in late 2027.

Marcus Webb will have transferred by then. His orders run through 2028. He's hoping to get stationed somewhere with better housing options.

"Somewhere that's not a motel," he said.

He went back inside Room 214. The door had one of those automatic closers on it. It shut slowly behind him.
